The statement is modestly hawkish and growth-negative. By lifting the federal funds target to 4.75–5.00% and maintaining balance-sheet runoff caps ($60B Treasuries, $35B MBS), the FOMC is operating in clearly restrictive territory, broadly consistent with Taylor-rule guidance historically associated with bringing down inflation. At the same time, the Committee flags tighter credit conditions from recent banking stress. Academic evidence on the credit and bank-lending channels (e.g., Bernanke-Blinder; Bernanke-Gertler) indicates such tightening can amplify the real effects of rate hikes via agency-cost and balance-sheet mechanisms, implying a larger drag on investment and employment than the standard interest-rate channel alone. The operational details—raising IOER to 4.9% and setting ON RRP at 4.8%—fit modern corridor/floor frameworks in which central banks steer short-term rates to transmit policy (as in the Fed’s use of administered rates). While liquidity backstops and lender-of-last-resort tools help contain systemic risk, literature on financial crises suggests that when banks retrench, macro effects can be material even if the system is “sound and resilient.” Net: downside risk to growth and hiring with disinflation likely to follow, offset by a credible anti-inflation stance.
